Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

could you draft a standalone fictional episode about a coastal cleanup from these notes? it should read as one complete episode, not a report about the whole town or a general guide to volunteering. the scene is gull point on a saturday in late september, with the work running from 8:30 in the morning until 12:15. the beach is a crescent below a low bluff, and the public access path comes down beside the closed tide kiosk. there was a light overnight rain, then gray clouds and a brisk wind from the water. the tide was falling when people arrived. no need to name a year or explain the wider history of the coast.

mara ellis is coordinating for the small volunteer group shorehands. she has a clipboard, a blue rain shell, and a roll of orange marking tape. she is practical and a little self-conscious about giving directions, but she knows where the supplies are. dev patel is a regular who brought a hand scale and a thermos; he is patient with new volunteers and keeps checking the time because he has to leave before noon. jo kim is a high school student who came with her aunt lena. jo is observant and takes photographs on an old silver camera, while lena is quiet and has a sore left wrist, so she sorts light items rather than lifting full bags. elias rowe, who runs the bait shop by the access road, lends two buckets and stops in briefly, but he is not part of the group and doesn't stay to work. there are nine volunteers altogether, but don't invent names or backstories for the other five.

supplies at the start are twelve pairs of gloves, eight reusable sacks, two buckets from elias, a first-aid pouch, a printed map, and one small scale. mara has a sign-in sheet but doesn't have a printed safety briefing. she gives a short spoken reminder to avoid sharp objects, leave wildlife alone, and call her over for anything that might be hazardous. nobody is hurt. show people working carefully and sorting what they can identify, but don't turn it into a dramatic rescue or a big confrontation. they find bottle caps, food wrappers, fishing line, fragments of foam, a cracked red sandal, and a plastic crate wedged near the rocks. the crate is too awkward to move safely with the people and equipment there, so they mark its location with orange tape and leave it for a later assessment. don't say who will collect it or when that will happen.

there are two different running counts in the notes: dev's tally at 10:40 says 17 kilograms in the sacks and buckets, while mara's end-of-morning sheet says 19 kilograms collected. keep both figures and make clear who recorded each and when; the notes don't explain the difference. the 19 kilograms excludes the crate, which remains in place. the group has collected 11 sacks' worth by the end, even though there were only eight reusable sacks at the start, because some were emptied and reused. don't suggest they had extra sacks. three bags of sorted material are set beside the access path for the municipal pickup, which is due on monday according to the printed map. two bags are ordinary waste, and one contains recyclables. the map also marks a storm drain near the top of the path. a volunteer spots a wrapper beside it, and jo photographs it before it is picked up. don't claim anything went into the drain.

use ordinary dialogue and include these exact quotations, attributed to the named speakers: mara says, “Take the line slowly; it can catch on the stones.” dev says, “I have ten minutes, and I can still finish this section.” jo says, “The tide is making the smaller pieces easier to see.” elias says, “Those buckets have a crack, so don't fill them to the rim.” lena says, “I can sort the light things here.” the wording should not be polished into different quotations. you can add a small amount of dialogue that follows naturally from the notes, but don't have anyone announce a lesson or deliver a speech.

rough sequence: people sign in at the kiosk, mara gives the safety reminder, and pairs spread out along the crescent. show the falling tide exposing more small debris, jo taking a few photographs, and lena sorting light items. dev weighs the collected material and records his 10:40 figure. elias drops off the buckets and gives his warning about the crack, then leaves. the group notices the crate near the rocks and marks it instead of trying to drag it away. later they gather by the path, separate the three bags for pickup, and mara makes her end-of-morning entry. dev leaves before noon. the cleanup ends at 12:15, but no final pickup or later assessment occurs in this episode.

Give the episode a simple title and include a numbered section labeled “1. The cleanup.” Keep the rest in ordinary prose rather than turning it into a checklist. Focus on this one morning and the interactions among the people; do not make it a report about the whole town or a general volunteering guide. Do not name a year or explain the coast’s wider history.

**Setting and participants**

The cleanup takes place at Gull Point on a Saturday in late September, from 8:30 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. The beach is a crescent below a low bluff. A public access path descends beside the closed tide kiosk. There was light rain overnight, followed by gray clouds and a brisk wind from the water. The tide is falling when the volunteers arrive.

Mara Ellis coordinates the small volunteer group Shorehands. She carries a clipboard, wears a blue rain shell, and has a roll of orange marking tape. She is practical and somewhat self-conscious about giving directions, but knows where the supplies are. Dev Patel is a regular volunteer who brought a hand scale and a thermos. He is patient with new volunteers and keeps checking the time because he must leave before noon. Jo Kim, a high school student, came with her aunt Lena. Jo is observant and takes photographs with an old silver camera. Lena is quiet and has a sore left wrist, so she sorts light items rather than lifting full bags. Elias Rowe runs the bait shop by the access road. He lends the group two buckets and stops briefly, but is not a member of the group and does not stay to work. There are nine volunteers altogether; do not invent names or backstories for the other five.

**Supplies and safety**

At the start, the group has twelve pairs of gloves, eight reusable sacks, two buckets borrowed from Elias, a first-aid pouch, a printed map, and one small scale. Mara has a sign-in sheet but no printed safety briefing. She gives a short spoken reminder: avoid sharp objects, leave wildlife alone, and call her over about anything that might be hazardous. Nobody is hurt. Show the volunteers working carefully and sorting items they can identify. Do not introduce a dramatic rescue or major confrontation.

The volunteers find bottle caps, food wrappers, fishing line, foam fragments, a cracked red sandal, and a plastic crate wedged near the rocks. The crate is too awkward to move safely with the people and equipment present. They mark its location with orange tape and leave it for a later assessment. Do not state who will collect it or when.

**Collection notes and sequence**

The notes contain two different running weights. At 10:40, Dev records 17 kilograms in the sacks and buckets. At the end of the morning, Mara’s sheet records 19 kilograms collected. Include both figures, with their respective recorders and times, and leave the difference unexplained. The 19 kilograms excludes the crate, which remains in place. By the end, the volunteers have collected 11 sacks’ worth. They started with eight reusable sacks because some were emptied and reused; do not imply they had extra sacks.

Three bags of sorted material are left beside the access path for municipal pickup, which the printed map says is due on Monday. Two bags contain ordinary waste and one contains recyclables. The map also marks a storm drain near the top of the path. A volunteer spots a wrapper beside the drain, and Jo photographs it before it is picked up. Do not claim that anything went into the drain.

Follow this rough sequence: the volunteers sign in at the kiosk; Mara gives the safety reminder; pairs spread out along the crescent. Show the falling tide exposing more small debris, Jo taking a few photographs, and Lena sorting light items. Dev weighs the collected material and records his 10:40 figure. Elias drops off the buckets, warns the group about the crack, and leaves. Later, the group notices the crate near the rocks and marks it rather than trying to drag it away. The volunteers gather by the path, separate the three bags for pickup, and Mara makes her end-of-morning entry. Dev leaves before noon. The cleanup ends at 12:15. No pickup or later assessment takes place during the episode.

**Dialogue and ending**

Include these exact quotations and attribute each to the named speaker:

- Mara: “Take the line slowly; it can catch on the stones.”
- Dev: “I have ten minutes, and I can still finish this section.”
- Jo: “The tide is making the smaller pieces easier to see.”
- Elias: “Those buckets have a crack, so don't fill them to the rim.”
- Lena: “I can sort the light things here.”

Do not change the wording of these quotations. A small amount of additional dialogue is acceptable if it follows naturally from the notes, but nobody should announce a lesson or deliver a speech.
